newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar to edge higher during Asian trade.
newsitem.headline: Dollar to edge higher during Asian trade.

text.p: The dollar is expected to be range-bound but to edge slowly higher against both the yen and mark during Asian trade on Wednesday after slipping against the mark in overseas trade on Tuesday, when Japanese markets were closed for a holiday.

The release on Tuesday of surprisingly weak U.S. economic data had dimmed expectations of a near-term interest rate hike and set off dollar sales against the mark. On Monday, the greenback hit 1.7395 marks, its highest since February 1994.
Against the yen, rises will be blocked by options-linked sales near 127.30 yen and other offers near 127.10 yen.

Dealers said the dollar's moves against the yen in particular are likely to be a tug-of-war between buying interest on the back of a lack of concrete measures to prevent dollar rises after the Group of Seven (G7) meeting last weekend, and concerns about possible dollar-selling intervention should the greenback rise suddenly.
Some exporter selling of dollars for yen is possible at the highs, but volume is unlikely to be large, dealers added.
Should the greenback manage to break above 127.30 yen, stop-loss buying could emerge near 127.35 yen. But dealers said this appears unlikely in Asia today.

The U.S. Labour Department reported on Tuesday that the first quarter employment cost index rose 0.6 percent, below Wall Street forecasts of a 0.9 percent rise. Later, the Commerce Department reported that durable goods orders dropped 3.0 percent, the largest drop since August 1996 and below expectations of a flat reading.

This dimmed expectations about a near-term rise in U.S. interest rates and prompted sales of dollars for marks by investors who had hoped to capitalise on a rising interest-rate gap between the U.S. and Germany. But the dollar later recovered slightly on a U.S. asset market rally in late trade.

Tokyo dealers said the dollar's recovery against the mark were likely to be limited in Asia, but that the greenback could start rising again once European trading begins. "Yesterday's moves may well have been more book-squaring than anything," one dealer said.
The market will be watching the behaviour of sterling ahead of the May 1 British election, with moves likely to be limited during Asian trading time.
